title: Why AI has a weird attention span you must learn to manage · hancrafted
description: AI's attention span, its context window, is a limited resource you have to actively manage: one chat per job, a handoff after real progress or before a break, and for bigger projects one planner chat that hands each step to a fresh chat.

Everyday habits Length itself hurts With perfect retrieval, performance still dropped as input grew, and the drop persisted when irrelevant tokens were replaced by whitespace or masked from attention 1 ; that a fresh, shorter chat avoids the drop is an inference from this, the studies do not test a restart. Sources (1) Du et al., Context Length Alone Hurts LLM Performance Despite Perfect Retrieval ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org One job per chat Even a single distractor lowers performance relative to the needle alone, so unrelated material in a chat has a cost 1 . Sources (1) Hong, Troynikov, Huber, Context Rot: How Increasing Input Tokens Impacts LLM Performance ( opens in a new tab ) trychroma.com A short recap helped Having the model recite the retrieved evidence before solving, which turns a long task into a short one, improved results 1 ; that a handoff works the same way is an inference. Sources (1) Du et al., Context Length Alone Hurts LLM Performance Despite Perfect Retrieval ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org

The workflow for bigger projects Clean windows for each part Anthropic's remedy for long tasks includes sub-agents that work with clean windows 1 . Sources (1) Anthropic, Effective context engineering for AI agents ( opens in a new tab ) anthropic.com Short tasks beat long ones Turning a long task into a short one improved results, GPT-4o on RULER by up to 4% 1 . Sources (1) Du et al., Context Length Alone Hurts LLM Performance Despite Perfect Retrieval ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org

The long phone call 0:00 – 0:33 A long chat is a long call Imagine the last long phone call you had with someone close, a sister, a friend, your mum. You called to settle one thing, and an hour later you hung up. Before I say a word about AI, I want you to feel what that call left you with, because the question I want to ask you is whether a long AI chat does the same thing to you, so the call comes first and the chat second.

The AI's attention span 0:00 – 0:17 Why it happens So far you have seen what happens. Now the cause, because once you know how the AI holds a chat, the pattern stops being a surprise, and only after that do we look at what it does to your answers.

What fills the window 0:00 – 0:13 More in there than you typed You have seen the window fill with your messages. But your messages are only a part of it, so the next question is what else goes in without you noticing.
Managing the attention span 0:00 – 0:09 You manage by habit You can't read a gauge, so you build habits. First the everyday ones, and then the one for a big project.

Everyday habits 0:00 – 0:11 Break it down Break it down. You know this one already: you split a big task into small steps, and each step is small enough to hold in view. 0:11 – 0:24 Fresh start Fresh start. You know this one too: a fresh start spends the whole window on the work in front of you, and none of it on what happened an hour ago. 0:24 – 0:35 One chat, one job One chat, one job. When the topic changes, open a new chat, so that the hotel question doesn't have to carry the catering PDF along. 0:35 – 0:49 Ask for a handoff Ask for a handoff. After real progress, or before a coffee break, stop and ask the AI for a handoff: a short card with the goal, what is decided and what comes next. 0:49 – 1:02 Read and correct it Then read it and correct what is wrong. A summary can leave things out or get one wrong, and you are the one accountable for what the next chat believes. 1:02 – 1:18 Start the next chat with it And start the next chat with it. Paste the handoff in as the first message, and the new chat starts small and sharp, with the venue, the caterer, the budget and the next step, and nothing else.

The workflow for bigger projects 0:00 – 0:13 One chat is too small Sometimes the project is bigger than one chat can hold: the whole summer party, with venues, catering, hotels and invitations. One chat would fill up, whatever window size you give it. 0:13 – 0:32 Break it down first So you break it down first. Work backward from the outcome, what do I need to run this party, and then what do I need for that, until the next step is clear. You can ask the AI to help you with that. 0:32 – 0:42 One planner Then one chat stays the planner. It keeps only the plan and the results, so it stays small and has room to spare. 0:42 – 1:01 A fresh chat per step Each step goes to a fresh chat: venues, catering, invitations. That chat reads its files and fills up as much as it needs, hands the result back to the planner as one small card, and then you let it go. Next step, next fresh chat. 1:01 – 1:47 You coordinate And you coordinate, like a project manager. This is what we call a workflow. Every chat has one job, so none of them runs long enough to blur its middle. That is the whole idea: the window is the AI's attention span, and managing it is your job. One honest caveat: the zones and numbers I gave you are rules of thumb and illustrations, and I have not tested every chat app, so watch your own chats and adjust. If you want a low-key place to start, take the next chat that drifts, ask it for a handoff, and open a new one with it. Thank you.
